conflicts.text: Firming the shock and running more rear pressure costs rear traction on loose climbs. Split the difference or accept one.
One wants the bike softer and more open, the other wants it firmer. These cancel. Pick the one that is actually costing you time.
Faster rebound gives pop but adds harshness and arm pump on long rough descents. One click at a time here.
Slower rebound calms the bike and takes the pop away. The rebound dial cannot give you both.
Platform for climbing is the same damping that makes the descent harsh. Consider using the lever rather than the tune.
Ramp and pressure changes for bottom out control sit against the softer rear you want for climbing grip.

diagnostics.test: Press the bars down hard and release
diagnostics.reads: Front wheel leaves the ground means rebound is too fast

diagnostics.test: Ride the same rough section twice, watch the o-ring
diagnostics.reads: Not reaching full travel on the biggest hit means too much ramp or too much pressure

diagnostics.test: Judge the bike entering a corner or on a jump face
diagnostics.reads: Sluggish and stacking up under you means low speed compression is too open
Harsh on quick impacts while barely using travel means high speed compression is too closed

diagnostics.test: Kerb drop, front and rear together
diagnostics.reads: Front and rear returning at visibly different speeds is the classic buck

diagnostics.test: Cycle the fork by hand, cold
diagnostics.reads: Notchiness off the top is mechanical, not tuning

sag_method.summary: Sag measurement gates everything else. Standing or seated both work, but pick one and never mix them, or readings across sessions are not comparable.
steps: Full kit on, including a pack if you ride with one.
Level ground. Do not hold the brakes; it loads the fork and gives a false reading.
Bounce a few times to free the seals, then settle into your normal riding stance.
Slide the o-ring down to the seal without shifting your weight.
Measure o-ring to seal, divide by total travel, multiply by 100.
